deep.reconstruction:
Setting (top right): x/(2π) = m/n with m/n in lowest terms. So e^{ix} is a primitive n-th root of unity and the angle is px/2 = π p m/n. The page belongs to Riemann's study of the radial limits of elliptic modular functions (series in q as q → e^{ix}). The next page treats Σ(−1)^s log(1+q^s)/s^2, the dilogarithm ϱ(x) = ∫_1^x log x dx/(1−x), and Σ 1/(ν+n)^2.

The page lists four expressions. Each is the value, at q = e^{ix}, of a series of the shape Σ_s F(s)/s^2 with F(s) = log|G(q^s)|^2. Three elementary identities (my addition) explain the integrands:
- |1+e^{isx}|^2 = 4 cos^2(sx/2), so log 4cos^2(sx/2) is log|1+q^s|^2.
- (1−e^{isx})/(1+e^{isx}) = −i tan(sx/2), so log tan^2(sx/2) is log|(1−q^s)/(1+q^s)|^2.
- |1−e^{isx}|^2 = 4 sin^2(sx/2).

Because F has period n in s, Riemann writes s = nt+p (or s = 2nt+p) and splits into residue classes.

(63), n odd: −Σ_{p=1..2n−1} Σ_{t=−∞..∞} log tan^2(px/2) / (2nt+p)^2.
(63), n even: −Σ_t Σ_{p=1..n−1} log tan^2(px/2) / (nt+p)^2.
(64), n odd: Σ_{p=1..2n−1} Σ_t log(4cos^2(px/2)) / (2nt+p)^2.
(64), n even: +Σ_{p=1..n−1} Σ_t log(4cos^2(px/2)) / (nt+p)^2.
(62): the heading 'n impar' is struck out; there is no content.

Why t runs over all of Z: the integrands are even in s. So a sum over s>0 equals one half of the sum over s ≠ 0 (my inference; the factor 1/2 is either absorbed or omitted).

Why the modulus is 2n for n odd and n for n even: most plausibly the original series runs over odd s only (theta/modulus products such as k' = Π((1−q^{2s−1})/(1+q^{2s−1}))^4). Then Riemann's Σ_{1,2n−1} and Σ_{1,n−1} would mean odd p only. Odd residues need modulus lcm(2,n), which is 2n for n odd and n for n even. An alternative reading is a factor (−1)^s, i.e. −q in place of q; this gives the same dichotomy, since (x+π)/2π = (2m+n)/2n.

Inner sums (my addition): Σ_t 1/(nt+p)^2 = π^2/(n^2 sin^2(πp/n)). So each double sum collapses to a finite trigonometric sum over p, for example Σ_p log(4cos^2(πpm/n)) · π^2/(n^2 sin^2(πp/n)). These are cotangent/Dedekind-type sums. The next page's computation of Σ 1/(ν+n)^2 via −∫_0^1 log x · x^{ν−1}/(1−x^n) dx, and of the dilogarithm at roots of unity, serves exactly this evaluation.

Upside-down scribble at the bottom: ∫^π e^{xi} e^{nxi} δ/(1−δe^{xi}) dx. This is a Fourier-coefficient extraction from the geometric series δ/(1−δe^{xi}) = Σ δ^k e^{(k−1)xi}; it is routine.
errors: Singular terms are not excluded. For n odd, p = n lies in the range 1..2n−1 and tan(πm) = 0, so log tan^2 diverges. For n even, p = n/2 gives cos(πm/2) = 0 (m odd), so log(4cos^2) diverges. These are exactly the terms where q^s = ±1, the source of the radial singularity. Riemann presumably treats them separately, but the page does not say so.
The passage from Σ_{s>0} to Σ_{t∈Z} requires a factor 1/2 (by evenness); no such factor is shown.
The parentheses in log tg (px/2)^2 are ambiguous; it must mean log(tan^2(px/2)), not tan of (px/2)^2.

The first line of (63) shows struck-out marks and an uncertain denominator ('2' over an erased '3d'?). The exponent 2 on (2nt+p) appears to be missing in the first line, an evident slip by analogy with the others.

results.what: Splitting Σ_s F(s)/s^2 with n-periodic F (values of log|1±q^s| at q a root of unity) into residue classes, with the n-odd/n-even dichotomy
results.modern_name: Evaluation of Dirichlet series with periodic coefficients; radial limits of log-eta/theta series at roots of unity
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann's fragment on Grenzfälle der elliptischen Modulfunctionen (publ. 1876), with Dedekind's commentary (1877)

results.what: Σ_{t∈Z} 1/(nt+p)^2 = π^2/(n^2 sin^2(πp/n)), reducing the double sums to finite trigonometric (cotangent-type) sums
results.modern_name: Partial-fraction expansion of csc^2 / Hurwitz zeta at 2; precursor of Dedekind sums
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (csc^2 expansion); Dedekind (1877) for the sums arising from Riemann's fragment

deep.surprise_reason: These are working notes for Riemann's published fragment on the limiting cases of modular functions. Dedekind's commentary on that fragment is the known origin of Dedekind sums. Nothing here goes beyond what is known to be Riemann's.

checkable.asserts: Inner sum over t equals π^2/(n^2 sin^2(πp/n))

checkable.sympy: m,n=1,5; x=2*pi*m/n; S1=nsum(lambda s: log(4*cos(s*x/2)**2)/s**2 if s%(2*n)!=0 else 0,[-inf,inf]); S2=sum(log(4*cos(p*x/2)**2)*pi**2/((2*n)**2*sin(pi*p/(2*n))**2) for p in range(1,2*n)); abs(S1-S2)<1e-8
checkable.asserts: The n-odd form of (64) equals the finite trigonometric sum obtained by summing over t first

transcription_corrections: (63) first line: there are struck-out marks before Σ^p ('−2'/'Σs' crossed) and after Σ^t; the denominator of the angle is 2, overwritten on an erased symbol; the exponent 2 on (2nt+p) is apparently missing in the manuscript.
Read 'log tg (px/2)^2' as log(tan^2(px/2)) and 'log 4 cos (px/2)^2' as log(4cos^2(px/2)).
Σ_{1,2n−1} and Σ_{1,n−1} may denote sums over odd p only (Riemann's usual notation); this is not certain.
The bottom upside-down line reads approximately ∫^π e^{xi}, e^{nxi} ∂x · δ/(1−δe^{xi}); the lower limit is illegible (possibly −π).
